passage: On the crowded evening metro, Arnab noticed the man in the grey jacket again. He had been standing too close to Gopika, Arnab's classmate, for two stations, leaning in whenever the train swayed and muttering something. Gopika kept shifting her bag in front of her, jaw tight. Arnab's first urge was to shout at him. Instead he moved beside her and asked quietly, "Hey, is this guy bothering you? Do you want me to stand here, get off with you, or tell the guard? Your call." Gopika breathed out. "Just stand here. And get off with me at the next stop." On the platform she said, "I want to report it, but I want to do it myself." Arnab waited while she spoke to the station security officer, and only added what he had seen when she asked him to.

qa.q: What options did Arnab offer Gopika?
qa.a: To stand there, get off with her, or tell the guard: "Your call."

qa.q: What was Arnab's first urge, and why might he have held it back?
qa.a: His first urge was to shout at the man; he held back so Gopika could decide what she wanted instead of having a scene made around her.

qa.q: Why did Arnab only add what he had seen when Gopika asked?
qa.a: It kept the report in Gopika's hands, so the help supported her choice instead of taking over.

qa.q: How might Gopika have felt being asked "Your call"?
qa.a: She probably felt respected and less helpless, able to choose what would make her feel safe.

grounding: A young man who sees a classmate harassed on the metro asks her privately what she wants and follows her lead in reporting it.

passage:
"Anju, can I come in?" Elizabeth knocked on the half-open door.
Anjali was on her bed, phone face down. "You saw it."
"I saw it. What Vikas posted under your photo was disgusting. I wanted to reply to him in the group right away."
"Please don't."
"I didn't. That's why I'm here. I don't want to decide this for you. What do you want? We can report it to the warden, or to the college committee. I can come with you. Or I can just sit here and we eat biscuits and hate him."
Anjali laughed a little, then her eyes filled. "I want it gone. But I don't want a big fight in the group."
"Okay. We take screenshots, then you report it through the committee form. I'll sit with you while you fill it in."
"Tonight?"
"Whenever you say."
Anjali turned her phone over. "Tonight."

qa.q: Where did Vikas post his comment?
qa.a: Under Anjali's photo, in the group.

qa.q: Why did Anjali say "Please don't" so quickly?
qa.a: She was afraid of a big public fight in the group, which would put even more attention on her.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth choose to do instead of replying in the group, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Elizabeth came to ask what Anjali wanted and offered options, so Anjali stayed in control of how it was handled.

qa.q: How might Vikas be affected by a committee report rather than a public reply?
qa.a: A report means Vikas faces a proper process, not a public shouting match he could enjoy or twist around.

grounding: A friend who saw someone harassed online checks privately what she wants, offers reporting or company, and lets her choose.

passage: At the college fest last spring, I watched three guys from another department follow Kavitha from the food stalls to the stage, calling out comments about her dress. I was furious. My plan was to march up and tell them off in front of everyone. But I remembered the time someone "defended" me by yelling at a boy in the canteen, and how everyone then stared at me, not him. So I waited until Kavitha stepped behind the stage and asked, "Those guys are being gross. What would help? Leave, report them, or I just stick next to you?" Kavitha thought for a second. "Stick next to me. If they come back, we'll tell the fest volunteers." They came back once. We told the volunteers together. I'm Shalini, by the way. Kavitha still calls me her bodyguard, which isn't quite right. I was more like the extra seat.

qa.q: What were the three guys calling out about?
qa.a: Comments about Kavitha's dress.

qa.q: Why did Shalini decide not to march up and tell them off?
qa.a: Shalini was furious but remembered being "defended" loudly in the canteen and how everyone stared at the target, and didn't want that for Kavitha.

qa.q: What made Shalini's question behind the stage a good turning point?
qa.a: It offered clear choices, leave, report or company, and let Kavitha pick, so the help followed her lead.

qa.q: What does Kavitha calling Shalini a "bodyguard" suggest about how she experienced the help?
qa.a: She felt protected and not alone, even though what Shalini really did was stay beside her and follow her plan.

grounding: A young adult who witnesses a friend being harassed asks her privately what would help and follows her choice rather than taking over.

passage:
Warden's note, college mess, Thursday.
At dinner a final-year student at the next table kept commenting on Zeenat's kurta and telling her to "turn around, let's see". Several people looked away. Chinmay, from her lab batch, stood up, and I expected shouting. There was none. He walked Zeenat to the water cooler and, from where I stood, I heard him ask, "Do you want me to say something, report it, or just sit with you?" She said, "Just sit. I'll decide later." He sat with her until she finished eating and did not look at the other table once.
Friday morning, Zeenat came to my office, with Chinmay waiting outside. She wanted to file a complaint. I thanked her for coming, told her none of it was her fault, and forwarded it to the college's harassment committee the same day. I have asked Chinmay whether he would give a statement, if Zeenat wishes.

qa.q: What three options did Chinmay offer Zeenat?
qa.a: Whether to say something, report it, or just sit with Zeenat.

qa.q: Why might Zeenat have answered, "Just sit. I'll decide later"?
qa.a: Zeenat was probably shaken and needed calm company first, while wanting to keep the decision about reporting firmly in Zeenat's own hands.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Chinmay's choice, and why did it help?
qa.a: Chinmay stood up looking ready to confront, but instead asked Zeenat privately what help was wanted, so control stayed with Zeenat, who chose to report the next morning.

qa.q: How did the warden's view of Chinmay shift during that dinner?
qa.a: The warden first expected shouting, then saw a quieter kind of help, and trusted Chinmay enough to ask for a statement, but only if Zeenat wishes.

grounding: A peer who sees a classmate harassed in the mess checks privately what help is wanted, leaving the choice to report with the person affected.

passage:
Wednesday night
At the site office today the contractor did it again. Anirban bent to pick up the drawings and the man said, "Careful, madam," in that sing-song voice, then blocked the doorway with an arm so Anirban had to squeeze past. Two workers laughed. My whole body wanted to walk up and yell. I had the words ready.
But I remembered how Anirban goes quiet when people fuss. So at lunch, behind the water tanks, I only asked: "That doorway thing. What do you want to do? I'll back whatever you pick, or nothing."
Anirban was silent a long time. Then: "Come with me to the coordinator tomorrow. Don't talk for me. Just be there."
So that's the plan. Writing it here so I don't forget: tomorrow my job is to stand next to him and keep my mouth shut.
Tanuja

qa.q: Where did Tanuja ask Anirban what to do?
qa.a: At lunch, behind the water tanks.

qa.q: What did Tanuja want to do at the doorway, and what held that urge back?
qa.a: Tanuja felt angry and wanted to walk up and yell at the contractor, but remembered that Anirban goes quiet when people fuss, and held back from taking over.

qa.q: Why was Tanuja's question at lunch the right turning point?
qa.a: By offering to back "whatever you pick, or nothing", Tanuja let Anirban decide, and Anirban chose a clear plan: company at the coordinator's office without being spoken for.

qa.q: How might Anirban experience going to the coordinator with Tanuja present but silent?
qa.a: Anirban gets support while staying the one who tells the story, which likely feels steadier than being rescued in front of the men who laughed 🤍

grounding: A peer who sees Anirban harassed at a work site checks privately what help is wanted and agrees to come along without speaking for the person affected.
